title: Completion at a principal regular maximal ideal is a DVR
statement: Let $S$ be a nonzero commutative local ring, meaning a ring with exactly one maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$. Suppose $\mathfrak m=tS$ for an element $t\in S$ such that multiplication by $t$ on $S$ is injective. Write $D=\varprojlim_{n\geq1}S/t^nS$ for its completion [def-weil-pbc-adically-complete-ring], and $\widehat t$ for the image of $t$ in $D$. Then $D$ is a discrete valuation ring [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring], complete for its maximal ideal, and that maximal ideal is $\widehat tD$, with $\widehat t\neq0$. Projection to the first component induces an isomorphism $D/\widehat tD\simeq S/tS$ compatible with the canonical map $S\to D$. No Noetherianity, domain, or separatedness assumption on $S$ is imposed.

source.place: Tag 0328 (lemma-cohen-rings-exist), proof of the completion step, generalized from the regular element p to an arbitrary regular generator t of the maximal ideal. The generalization is written by Q20; locality and the quotient of the completion are the same ones used there.

proof.text: Put $I=tS$. Since $\mathfrak m=tS$, $I$ is finitely generated and $S/I$ is a field. The completion in the statement is the $I$-adic completion because $I^n=t^nS$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-adic-completion-mod-ideal]: the first-coordinate projection $\pi:D\to S/tS$ is surjective, has kernel $ID=\widehat tD$, and induces $D/\widehat tD\simeq S/tS$ compatibly with $S\to D$; the same result says that $D$ is $ID$-adically complete.

source.place: Tag 05GG, parts (1)--(2), applied to I=(t); Tag 0328, completion step

proof.text: The ideal $\widehat tD=ID$ is maximal because its quotient is the field $S/tS$. The Jacobson-radical completion lemma [lem-weil-pbc-adic-complete-jacobson-radical] puts $ID$ inside every maximal ideal of $D$. Hence every maximal ideal equals $ID$, so $D$ is local with maximal ideal $\widehat tD$. The $ID$-adic completeness from Step 1 is therefore completeness for its maximal ideal.

The element $t$ is nonzero: if $t=0$, injectivity of multiplication by $t$ gives $1=0$, contrary to $S
e0$. It is not a unit because $tS=\mathfrak m$ is a proper maximal ideal. Also $t

source.place: Tag 0328, completion step; cancellation by the regular generator

proof.text: Multiplication by $\widehat t$ on $D$ is injective. If $\widehat t x=0$, choose a representative $a_{n+1}\in S$ of the $(n+1)$st component of $x$. The $(n+1)$st component of the equality says $ta_{n+1}\in t^{n+1}S$. Injectivity of multiplication by $t$ on $S$ then gives $a_{n+1}\in t^nS$, so the $n$th component of $x$ is zero. This holds for every $n$, and equality in the inverse limit is componentwise.

source.place: Tag 0328, completion step; direct cancellation in the inverse-limit components

proof.text: The filtration by powers of $\widehat tD$ is separated: the $ID$-adic completeness from Step 1 includes the assertion that an element lying in every $(\widehat tD)^n$ is zero. Therefore a nonzero $x\in D$ misses some power. Choose the least $r\ge0$ with $x\in(\widehat tD)^r$ but $x\notin(\widehat tD)^{r+1}$, and write $x=\widehat t^{\,r}y$. Then $y\notin\widehat tD$, so its nonzero image in the field $D/\widehat tD$ makes $y$ a unit (Step 2). Thus every nonzero element is a power of $\widehat t$ times a unit.

source.place: Tag 00PD, unit-times-uniformizer-power argument, with separatedness from Tag 05GG

proof.text: If $xy=0$ and $x,y\ne0$, factor them as $x=\widehat t^{\,r}u$ and $y=\widehat t^{\,s}v$ by Step 5. The injectivity in Step 4 makes every power of $\widehat t$ injective, and cancellation of the units $u,v$ then contradicts $x,y\ne0$. Hence $D$ has no zero divisors; it is nontrivial because $S/tS$ is a nonzero field. Thus $D$ is a domain. The nonzero element $\widehat t$ lies in its maximal ideal, so $D$ is not a field.

source.place: Tag 00PD, implications of the unit-times-uniformizer-power factorization

proof.text: Let $J\subseteq D$ be an ideal. If $J=0$ it is principal. Otherwise choose a nonzero element of $J$ with least exponent $r$ in Step 5. Every nonzero $z\in J$ has exponent $s\ge r$, hence $z=\widehat t^{\,r}(\widehat t^{\,s-r}w)$ for a unit $w$; the chosen element generates $\widehat t^{\,r}D$, so $J=\widehat t^{\,r}D$. Therefore every ideal is principal. Together with the domain and local properties, the nonzero maximal ideal $\widehat tD$ and the definition [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring] show that $D$ is a discrete valuation ring. Step 1 already gives the asserted completeness and quotient compatibility.
